mcq: Which property defines a ribozyme?
Catalysis by RNA|Any RNA that binds a metabolite|Translation of RNA|Any RNA with a stem
Catalysis requires acceleration of a chemical transformation. Binding, being translated and forming a stem do not establish catalytic activity.
Which classical bacterial RNA processes the 5′ end of pre-tRNA?
5S rRNA|M1 RNA of RNase P|U1 snRNA|tRNA anticodon
M1 RNA is the catalytic RNA component of E. coli RNase P. 5S rRNA is ribosomal, U1 recognizes splice sites and the anticodon participates in decoding.
The usual RNase P cleavage leaves which end on mature tRNA?
5′ hydroxyl|3′ cyclic phosphate|5′ phosphate|5′ cap
Hydrolysis produces the mature 5′ phosphate and a leader with a 3′ hydroxyl. A cyclic phosphate and 5′ hydroxyl are characteristic of many self-cleavers.
Which group initiates conventional group I intron splicing?
ATP γ-phosphate|Intronic adenosine 2′ OH|Water in all cases|External guanosine 3′ OH
The external guanosine supplies the nucleophile; branch-site adenosine is typical of group II and spliceosomal branching. GTP hydrolysis is not the driving chemistry.
The canonical group II lariat contains which unusual linkage?
2′–5′ phosphodiester|5′–5′ triphosphate|Peptide bond|3′–3′ disulfide
The branch A uses its 2′ oxygen to link to the intron 5′ end. The cap linkage is different; peptide and disulfide bonds are protein chemistry.
Which component supplies the bacterial peptidyl-transferase center?
16S rRNA|23S rRNA|5S rRNA alone|Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase
The large subunit 23S rRNA forms the catalytic environment. 16S rRNA is in the small subunit; synthetases charge tRNAs before translation.
A conventional small self-cleaving RNA generally generates which termini?
Two 5′ phosphates|3′ OH and 5′ phosphate|2′,3′ cyclic phosphate and 5′ OH|Two peptide ends
Attack by the upstream 2′ oxygen produces a cyclic phosphate and leaves the downstream 5′ hydroxyl. The hydrolysis termini in B describe RNase P instead.
What does a catalyst change?
The equilibrium constant invariably|The identity of every product|The total free energy of reactants alone|The activation barrier
Catalysts accelerate reaction pathways without altering the thermodynamic equilibrium under identical conditions. They need not alter final product identity or initial free energy.
Which RNA region directly recognizes a conventional riboswitch ligand?
Aptamer|Promoter DNA|Stop codon|Poly(A) tail
The aptamer provides the recognition pocket. The promoter controls initiation and the stop codon controls translation termination; neither defines the ligand receptor.
Which region converts recognition into a regulatory outcome?
Anticodon|Expression platform|Centromere|Histone tail
The platform couples ligand recognition to accessibility, termination or another expression event. The other structures have unrelated functions.
Where are many bacterial riboswitches located?
Within all tRNA anticodons|Only in genomic promoters|5′ untranslated regions of mRNAs|Only in 3′ poly(A) tails
The 5′ leader is common in bacteria but not universal; eukaryotic regulatory RNA examples occupy other locations.
Which RNA structure most directly promotes intrinsic bacterial termination in the standard model?
Aminoacyl-tRNA|A stop codon alone|A 5′ cap|Hairpin followed by a U-rich tract
The stem-loop and downstream uridines contribute to release of the transcription complex. A stop codon acts at translation.
A ligand-bound translational OFF switch typically does what?
Sequesters the ribosome-binding region|Excises every intron|Blocks all transcription initiation|Chemically modifies genomic DNA
The coding RNA can still be synthesized; initiation becomes inefficient because an RNA region becomes inaccessible.
What is TPP?
A purine base|A thiamine-derived cofactor|A ribosomal protein|A DNA polymerase
TPP is thiamine diphosphate, a cofactor in metabolism. It is not a protein or nucleobase.
What is FMN derived from?
Thymine|Glucose alone|Riboflavin|Methionine
Flavin mononucleotide is a vitamin B2 derivative involved in redox chemistry. SAM, not FMN, is derived from methionine.
Which signal activates the natural glmS ribozyme?
Adenine|TPP|FMN|Glucosamine-6-phosphate
Glucosamine-6-phosphate stimulates glmS RNA cleavage. Other ligands have their own switch families.
What is demonstrated by ligand binding to a purified aptamer alone?
Recognition capacity|Protein output necessarily changes|All transcripts terminate|The RNA necessarily catalyzes cleavage
A binding assay establishes association under tested conditions, not a regulatory or catalytic outcome without additional evidence.
Which statement about Mg²⁺ and catalytic RNA is correct?
Mg²⁺ is consumed once per peptide bond|It may support folding and/or catalytic chemistry|Every RNA that binds Mg²⁺ is a riboswitch|It replaces the RNA backbone
Metal ions help stabilize RNA and can participate in chemistry. Neither a universal stoichiometric consumption nor a sensing function follows from their presence.
Which is an established protein-only exception to RNA-based RNase P?
E. coli M1 RNA|Tetrahymena group I intron|Human mitochondrial RNase P|Bacterial 23S rRNA
Human mitochondrial RNase P is protein-based; the other named RNA catalysts illustrate different reactions.
What is the expected immediate group I excised intron product?
A peptide|A lariat in every case|Only mononucleotides|Typically a linear RNA with the incorporated guanosine
The standard group I transesterifications yield a linear intron. Some introns rearrange or circularize subsequently.
Which statement about riboswitch direction is correct?
Both activation and repression are possible|Every switch is OFF|Every switch is ON|Binding necessarily changes the DNA sequence
The expression platform determines the sign of regulation. Binding need not change DNA or create a new RNA sequence.
Why is an untranslated region capable of regulation?
It is always removed|Its sequence can fold and control RNA accessibility or processing|It encodes every protein|It cannot interact with molecules
An untranslated sequence can carry structural and recognition information independent of translation into amino acids.
What does cis regulation mean in the typical riboswitch context?
The ligand is always covalently linked to the switch|The RNA acts only on unrelated chromosomes|The element regulates expression of its own RNA molecule|The riboswitch is a protein
Cis describes the relationship between the regulatory element and the molecule carrying it, not whether the ligand is covalently attached.
Which observation provides direct evidence of RNA catalysis?
RNA is abundant in cells|RNA is sensitive to an RNase|RNA folds into a helix|Purified RNA accelerates specific product formation over background
A specific catalytic reaction by RNA is stronger evidence than abundance, structure or sensitivity to degradation.
ar: A bacterial RNase P RNA can be catalytic outside the intact complex.
An isolated bacterial RNase P RNA can process precursor tRNA under suitable ionic conditions.
Both statements are true; the isolated activity directly supports the assertion.
A ligand-binding mutation can remove riboswitch regulation.
The binding event is required for the normal response of a conventional ligand-dependent switch.
Both are true; without recognition the ligand cannot normally control the expression platform.
Some ligand-bound states favor transcription readthrough.
The assertion is false and the reason true. ON switches are a real counterexample.
The standard group II reaction generates a lariat.
An internal adenosine 2′ hydroxyl attacks the 5′ splice junction.
The chemical attack produces the branch that explains lariat formation.
The ribosome is a ribonucleoprotein complex.
RNA catalysts change the equilibrium constant of peptide bond synthesis.
The assertion is true; the reason is false. Catalysts change rates, not equilibrium.
An isolated aptamer can bind a ligand without its expression platform.
A transcriptional OFF switch may form an intrinsic terminator.
Both statements can be true, but the specific output does not explain the recognition ability of the isolated aptamer.
multi: Select the correct statements: I. Group I uses free G. II. Group II commonly uses branch A. III. Both normally require ATP ligase for exon joining.
I and II only|II and III only|I and III only|I, II and III
I and II describe the initiating nucleophiles. III is false: the second transesterification joins exons without a dedicated ATP-driven ligase.
Match 1 RNase P, 2 23S rRNA, 3 aptamer, 4 expression platform with a peptide bond, b ligand binding, c pre-tRNA 5′ processing, d regulatory output.
RNase P processes tRNA, 23S rRNA supplies the peptide-bond center, aptamers bind ligand and platforms control output.
Which are correct? I. TPP switches occur in plants. II. All riboswitches lie in bacterial 5′ UTRs. III. glmS can be both catalytic and regulatory.
I only|II and III|I and III|All three
I and III are established examples. II ignores eukaryotic processing switches and other locations.
Match 1 TPP, 2 FMN, 3 SAM, 4 GlcN6P with a methyl donor, b thiamine derivative, c flavin cofactor, d glmS activator.
The correct pairs connect each metabolite to its biochemical identity or established regulatory role.
Which statements are valid? I. Binding alone is not catalysis. II. Protein assistance does not exclude RNA catalysis. III. All RNA cleavage is hydrolysis.
I and II|II and III|I and III|III only
I and II distinguish function and sufficiency. III is false because many self-cleavers use transesterification.
pc: A 130-nt precursor contains a 38-nt 5′ leader. Correct RNase P cleavage yields what product lengths?
38 and 92 nt
130−38=92 nt. The leader and mature region account for the original 130 nucleotides. Cleavage itself adds no nucleotide.
An RNase P substrate is labeled only in the 5′ leader. Which product will a label-specific detector show after complete processing?
The released leader
The mature tRNA loses the labeled region. Absence of a visible mature tRNA in this detection mode is not evidence that processing failed.
A group I precursor has exons of 70 and 55 nt and an intron of 120 nt. One external guanosine is incorporated, with no secondary reaction. Predict the lengths of joined exons and excised intron.
125 and 121 nt
70+55=125; 120+1=121. Total product nucleotide count is 246, one more than the precursor because a guanosine was incorporated.
A group II intron contains 120 nt and its exons total 125 nt. What changes in nucleotide count when the intron branches and is excised?
No nucleotide is added; 120-nt intron and 125-nt joined exons
The 2′ hydroxyl belongs to an existing intron nucleotide. An unusual linkage is formed but no external nucleotide is incorporated in the standard branch pathway.
A group I mutant produces free 5′ exon and intron still linked to 3′ exon, but little joined exon product. Which step is impaired?
Second transesterification
The first reaction already generated the upstream exon hydroxyl. Its attack on the downstream junction has not occurred efficiently. Lack of initial free exon would indicate a first-step problem.
A ribozyme substrate binds mutant and wild type equally well, but the mutant makes no product. What can and cannot be concluded?
A post-binding defect is likely; direct catalytic atom assignment is not established
The observed binding rules out gross loss of affinity under the assay conditions. Misalignment, a defective chemical group or a subtle folding problem remain possible.
A stem mutation G–C→A–C abolishes ligand response; a second mutation yielding A–U restores response. What is supported?
The paired structure contributes to regulation
The rescue despite sequence change favors a pairing-dependent role. It does not prove the stem is the only structural requirement or that every alternative pair will work.
For Kd = 4 μM and free ligand 12 μM, find equilibrium fractional occupancy.
f=12/(4+12)=0.75. This applies to one-to-one equilibrium binding, not necessarily a cotranscriptional output.
At free ligand 0.25 μM, occupancy is 20%. Find Kd for the simple one-site model.
1 μM
For a switch whose unbound and bound outputs are 100 and 20 units, respectively, compute mean output when occupancy is 60%.
52 units
Y=0.40×100+0.60×20=40+12=52. Assuming 60% repression would ignore residual bound-state output.
A self-cleaving RNA follows first-order irreversible loss with k=0.10 min⁻¹. What fraction remains after 10 min?
P/P0=e^(−0.10×10)=e^(−1). Cleaved fraction is 63.2%, not 36.8%.
A homogeneous self-cleaving precursor has a 5-min half-life. Find its rate constant.
0.139 min⁻¹
k=ln 2/5≈0.1386 min⁻¹. The half-life is independent of starting concentration only under the assumed first-order model.
A nascent aptamer can bind for 80 nt of elongation at 40 nt s⁻¹. An additional 1-s pause falls entirely inside this window. What is the window?
3 s
80/40=2 s plus 1 s. Pauses outside the available binding interval would not necessarily add usable time.
Take kon=2 μM⁻¹ s⁻¹, ligand=0.5 μM and window=2 s. Under the encounter model with negligible dissociation, find binding probability.
About 0.865
kon[L]t=2×0.5×2=2; 1−e^(−2)=0.8647. This is not automatically termination probability.

Hypothetical transcription assay: 120 starts, 96 full-length without ligand and 30 full-length with ligand. Assuming all starts yield either full-length or terminated RNA, find termination percentages.
20% without ligand; 75% with ligand
Without ligand (120−96)/120=0.20; with ligand (120−30)/120=0.75. The change concerns elongation outcome, not initiation frequency.
A switch mutant binds FMN normally but produces nearly all full-length RNA regardless of ligand. Its terminator stem has been disrupted. Explain.
The output platform is defective, not necessarily the ligand receptor
Normal binding does not guarantee termination. Disrupting the required hairpin lets polymerase read through even in the bound state.
A ligand reduces protein 10-fold but full-length RNA remains constant. What additional observation would strengthen translational rather than protein-stability control?
Reduced initiation/ribosome occupancy at comparable RNA levels with protein stability controlled
Steady-state protein is determined by production and loss. A translation-specific observation is needed to separate the two explanations.
A glmS mutant binds metabolite but cannot self-cleave. Predict a result in a controlled cell-free cleavage assay and a plausible expression phenotype in cells.
Loss of ligand-induced fragments; impaired ligand-dependent repression
Recognition is not sufficient for cleavage-mediated turnover. Other cellular regulatory processes could affect expression, so the expression prediction should be tested.
An RNA-dependent enzyme loses activity with EDTA and regains it with Mg²⁺. Is direct participation of Mg²⁺ in catalysis proved?
No
Metal chelation may disturb folding, substrate binding or the chemical step. Independent structural and chemical evidence is required to locate its role.

Ligand A and B each have Kd=1 μM. A has fast association and dissociation; B has slow association and dissociation. Which necessarily binds more rapidly during a short initially unbound window at equal free concentration?
A has the larger initial association rate, but regulatory outcomes need not follow that order
Equal Kd fixes the ratio koff/kon, not the individual rates. Rapid binding is favored initially for A, but retention and coupling determine the ultimate output.
traps: Catalytic RNA is not synonymous with all ncRNA
Many functional RNAs are structural or regulatory without performing chemistry.
A riboswitch is not necessarily a ribozyme
Conventional switches act through binding and structural coupling; glmS is an overlapping case.
RNase P does not remove the 3′ end
Its classical processing reaction removes the 5′ leader of pre-tRNA.
Do not equate all RNase P systems
Bacterial RNA-based enzymes and protein-only human mitochondrial RNase P solve similar tasks.
A group I guanosine is not a GTP-powered motor
Its 3′ hydroxyl participates in transesterification.
A lariat is not a simple end-to-end circle
The group II branch is a 2′–5′ linkage.
The peptidyl-transferase center is not the small subunit
Bacterial 23S rRNA in the large subunit provides the catalytic architecture.
Binding does not demonstrate output
Aptamer and platform defects are separable.
A transcription terminator is not a stop codon
One concerns release of RNA polymerase; the other concerns translation termination.
Ligand binding does not always repress expression
ON and OFF outcomes depend on the platform.
Kd is not necessarily the reporter EC50
Timing, coupling and residual expression affect regulatory output.
A 5′ UTR is not the only possible location
Eukaryotic TPP riboswitches can regulate RNA processing from other positions.
RNA catalysis does not mean cellular protein independence
The reaction center and the functioning cellular complex must be distinguished.
Do not infer direct metal chemistry from chelation
Folding and catalysis can both depend on ions.
recall: How can RNA catalyze chemistry despite four standard bases?
Folding positions chemical groups, substrate and sometimes metal ions to favor reaction.
How do RNase P and self-cleaving ribozyme products differ?
RNase P gives 3′ OH/5′ phosphate; a typical small self-cleaver gives cyclic phosphate/5′ OH.
What initiates group I splicing?
External guanosine 3′ OH.
What initiates canonical group II splicing?
Internal branch-point adenosine 2′ OH.
What joins the exons in both pathways?
The upstream exon 3′ OH attacks the downstream junction.
What is the difference between an aptamer and a platform?
Recognition versus functional coupling to gene expression.
How is an OFF transcription switch different from a translational switch?
The first prevents complete RNA production; the second primarily reduces use of intact RNA.
Why can faster elongation affect riboswitch sensitivity?
It may shorten the time for folding and ligand association before commitment.
Which natural example links sensing directly to self-cleavage?
glmS, activated by glucosamine-6-phosphate.
What is needed to establish direct sensing?
Independent ligand binding, appropriate controls and evidence connecting recognition to the regulatory output.
